title: In This Town, Nobody Owns an Alarm Clock

lines.t: In this town, nobody owns an alarm clock. So you never wake up... until I shoot peas at you.
Three hundred people. Five mornings. Miss one sleepy head, and I lose five thousand dollars.
By Friday, there'd be a snoring Mayor, a pigeon that eats my ammo, and three hundred pairs of fluffy earmuffs.
And I'd finally find out why nobody here owns an alarm clock. The answer was in one attic.
It started on Sunday. The town's wake-up man, Old Gus, retired. He's ninety-four.
He fell asleep at his own retirement party. Nobody woke him up. That was kind of the problem.
Then the Mayor climbed on the stage and said: this Friday at six AM is the Sunrise Parade. Every single person must be awake.
Whoever wakes up the whole town, five mornings in a row, gets the job, five thousand dollars, and the Golden Pea Shooter.
I put my hand up. I'm eleven. I had one pea shooter and a bag of dried peas from Grandma's kitchen.
My best friend Benny laughed so hard he fell off his chair. He said: you can't even wake YOURSELF up.
The whole town laughed. Even the Mayor laughed. Then he wrote my name on the big screen anyway.
Which is fair. I've been late for school forty times. But I did my research.
This was a real job, by the way. In old Britain they were called knocker-ups. Some tapped windows with long sticks. One lady in London shot dried peas.
Each customer paid her sixpence a week. I wasn't getting sixpence. I was getting five thousand dollars.
Day one. Five AM. I climbed onto the bakery roof. First stop: the baker. Pea one. Tink.
He opened the window and threw a croissant at me. Which, honestly, was breakfast.
Then Grandma. Grandma sleeps with her eyes open. I shot nine peas before I realised she'd been awake the whole time, watching me.
House forty, the twins. Pea one wakes twin one. Twin one wakes twin two by sitting on him. Very efficient.
Two hundred and ninety eight. Two hundred and ninety nine. And then... Benny.
I shot a pea. Nothing. Ten peas. Nothing. I shot so many peas his window looked like a soup.
Benny slept until lunch. The Mayor wrote it on the big screen. Day one: two hundred ninety nine out of three hundred. One strike.
And Benny? Benny said he did it on purpose, to test me.
Day two. I brought a bigger bag of peas. And I made a new friend.
A pigeon. Every time I loaded a pea, the pigeon ate it. Load. Eat. Load. Eat.
By four fifty, I had zero peas and one very round pigeon.
It followed me home that night and slept on my windowsill. I named it Ammo.
So I ran home and grabbed the only thing left. Grandma's frozen peas. Frozen peas bounce. Frozen peas bounce LOUD.
Benny woke up in one shot. He was not happy. He was awake though.
Then I got to the Mayor's house. The Mayor snores so loud, his windows were already shaking. My peas couldn't hear themselves.
I climbed up to his open window. His mouth was wide open. I had one frozen pea left.
I want to say I aimed. I didn't aim. It just went in.
He sat straight up, coughed, and said: who's there? I said: room service. Day two: three hundred out of three hundred.
Day three. That's when Mrs. Pickles found out about the five thousand dollars.
Mrs. Pickles is undefeated at everything. Bingo, pie contests, staring contests with dogs.
And now she wanted my job. So she hung a giant net over the whole of Main Street. Every pea I shot bounced straight back at my face.
Pea. Ow. Pea. Ow. The pigeon thought it was a game.
Mrs. Pickles stood under the net in her bathrobe and said: give up, kid. Then one of my peas bounced off the net and landed in her curlers. She did not think that was a game.
So I went UP. I climbed every roof and dropped peas down the chimneys. Like Santa, but rude.
Three hundred chimneys. Two hours. My legs stopped talking to me.
Then Benny showed up with a ladder. He said: I'm not helping. I'm just holding this ladder. He held it for two hours.
But the screen said: three hundred out of three hundred. Mrs. Pickles looked at me like I'd stolen her bingo card.
Day four. Easy. Everybody woke up. Even Benny. Too easy.
The Mayor gave me a thumbs up from his window. He was chewing very carefully.
Because that evening, a truck drove down Main Street. Mrs. Pickles was handing out free gifts. Three hundred pairs of fluffy earmuffs.
The box said: sleep tight, love, Mrs. Pickles. Grandma put on two pairs.
That night, I couldn't sleep. Which, for me, is a first.
Tomorrow was the Sunrise Parade. The whole town would be wearing earmuffs. And peas don't go through fluff.
Day five. Four AM. I shot the baker's window. Nothing. Twenty peas at Benny. Nothing. The town was asleep and wrapped like burritos.
Five fifteen. Forty five minutes until the parade. The Mayor's big screen said: zero out of three hundred.
I sat on the curb. The pigeon sat next to me. For the first time all week, it didn't eat anything.
And then I smelled something. The bakery. The baker was the only one up, because the bakery opens at five, earmuffs or not.
Nobody in this town can hear through earmuffs. But everybody can smell cinnamon rolls.
I asked him for three hundred rolls. He said: who's paying? I said: the Golden Pea Shooter. He said: deal.
Then I dragged the giant fan from the summer fair to the middle of Main Street, pointed it at the bakery, and turned it on.
The smell went down the whole street. Doors opened. People came out in pyjamas, eyes closed, noses first.
Benny floated out like a cartoon. Grandma came out with both pairs of earmuffs still on. Even Mrs. Pickles came out. Holding a plate.
Then the Mayor. Still snoring. Walking. He's the only man in the world who can snore and walk at the same time.
Six AM. The Mayor counted. Two hundred ninety eight. Two hundred ninety nine...
And the screen stopped. Two hundred ninety nine out of three hundred. Somebody was missing.
Old Gus.
I ran to his house. Door open. Stairs. Attic. And there was Gus. Wide awake. Sitting by the window. With a pea shooter.
Pointed at MY bedroom window.
And behind him, the whole attic was full of alarm clocks. Hundreds of them. Every alarm clock this town ever bought.
Gus had been buying them up for seventy years, so the town would always need a wake-up man.
I said: Gus, that's cheating. He said: no, kid. That's business.
Then he said: kid, who do you think has been waking YOU up every morning this week?
Remember? I can't even wake myself up. I hadn't been late once all week. I thought I'd changed.
It was Gus. Every morning. Four thirty. One pea. Tink.
He walked to the parade with me. Three hundred out of three hundred. The whole town cheered with their mouths full.
I got the job, the five thousand dollars, and the Golden Pea Shooter. The pigeon got the leftover rolls.
Benny got a front row seat. He slept through the whole parade.
And Gus gave me a present. One alarm clock. He said: you'll need it. I'm retiring for real this time.
So now I'm the only person in this town with an alarm clock. I sleep right through it.
Should I keep the job? A, keep shooting peas. Or B, give everybody their alarm clocks back. Tell me in the comments.
